commenti.body:
The film intentionally does not reveal the nature of "space". This is more of a parable than a full-fledged story. Any of our assumptions in any case will be speculation. 

Nevertheless, for context, I can clarify the metaphysical meaning of the "space" set in the novel on the basis of which the film was made. In my opinion, the idea in the authors of the book (the Strugatsky Brothers) on this issue is deep enough, original and elegant to please you.

Not directly relevant to Stalker, which I feel does not accomodate any definitive answer on your question, but rather a couple of other films that do what you ask, that is bring people into abstracted spaces to explore them in relation to certain philosophical questions. 

***The Platform*** (El Hoyo) (2019) - A Spanish language film in which people are in a prison/experiment where the food is passed down from high to low on a platform. Explores justice/equity.

***Cube*** (1997) - Canadian horror sci-fi where people are trapped in a series of cube shaped rooms. Not very philosophical but there is a high degree of abstraction about mathematics mapping onto reality. 

***Next Floor*** (2007) - Denis Villeneuve short where people seem condemned to devour as much food as they can. No words, a silent portrayal of consumerism. 

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t60MMJH\_1ds

I'm sure by looking at these and other films set in a similar abstracted space you can get more inspiration than worrying at Stalker's 'hidden meaning' which I sincerely believe doesn't exist. 

IMO Stalker clearly says the Room is what you wish it to be, it contains what you wish it to contain, so all the possibilities you mention and more (the room is God, the room is a space that does not exist, etc) are true simultaneously. 

Hope that's helpful.
